La Converse est-elle un média « Ghetto »: Is La Converse a “Ghetto” Media Outlet?
Qualifier La Converse de « ghetto » revi: Calling La Converse a “ghetto” amounts to downplaying the impact of our work and misunderstanding our role in the media landscape.
L’équipe et les collègues de La Converse: The team and colleagues of La Converse, from left to right, top to bottom: Denitsa Hristova, Aude Simon, Laura Belfadla, Emelia Fournier, Firas Kefi, Maria Gabriela Aguzzi, Melissa Haouari, Loubna Chlaikhy, Lela Savić, Mouna Douab, Jennifer Da Veiga Rocha.
Récemment, j’ai eu l’occasion de rencont: Recently, I had the opportunity to meet with journalism students to introduce them to La Converse and the work we do as a media outlet.
Je leur ai exposé les raisons profondes: I explained the deeper reasons that drove me to create La Converse: the glaring lack of diversity in mainstream media; news coverage that is too rushed, often biased and leaves little room for introspection; and a tokenistic inclusion that confines people from diverse backgrounds to marginal roles. These dynamics contribute to an often traumatic relationship between marginalized communities and the media.
En m’appuyant sur mes observations sur l: Drawing on my observations in the field, on my experience as a <l1>Roma woman</l1> and on concrete examples such as the recommendations of the <l2>Bouchard-Taylor report</l2>, I sought to shed light on these systemic issues, which can no longer be ignored.
À un moment donné de la discussion avec: At one point in the discussion with the journalism students, the professor asked me a question. “You’re being harsh on traditional media by claiming that marginalized communities’ relationships with the media are traumatic. I find that you’ve given up on traditional media rather easily. Aren’t you afraid of creating a ‘ghetto media outlet’ where you would only be speaking to racialized people?”
Cette question m’a ramenée à la raison p: That question brought me back to the fundamental reason I decided to create La Converse, four years ago now. It highlights how important it is, today more than ever, to clarify what La Converse is, what it is not and why it plays an essential role in today’s media landscape.
Avant d’aller plus loin, prenons un inst: Before going any further, let’s take a moment to define the word “ghetto.” Originally, ghettos were the neighbourhoods reserved for Jews, where they were forced to live under segregation laws. The word was later used to describe places of forced exclusion, symbols of isolation and persecution. In North America, the term is often associated with disadvantaged Black neighbourhoods. According to the Larousse dictionary, “ghetto” refers to spaces where minorities live in isolation, generally because of economic pressures or systemic discrimination. Used as an adjective, it can also describe groups perceived as inward-looking. That is probably the sense in which the professor used it when he called La Converse a “ghetto media outlet.”
Cependant, le sociologue Loïc Wacquant r: However, sociologist Loïc Wacquant points out that this kind of usage can create a false impression. When the term “ghetto” is applied to initiatives or spaces led by marginalized groups, it reinforces the idea that they are isolated or divisive. Such an interpretation misses their essential role: giving marginalized communities the means to make themselves heard in a society where inequalities persist.
M. Wacquant souligne également que des e: Wacquant also notes that exclusive spaces created by privileged groups, such as wealthy, homogeneous suburbs, are never called “ghettos,” even though they display a social and cultural homogeneity similar to that of any ghetto. This asymmetry shows how steeped the use of the word is in judgment and social bias.
La Converse is not a ghetto. Calling La Converse a “ghetto” amounts to downplaying the impact of our work and misunderstanding our role in the media landscape. The term, historically marked by segregation and exclusion, implies that our legitimacy depends on frameworks imposed by dominant structures. It is time to let go of this misconception: when marginalized communities take their place, they are not creating ghettos. They are creating spaces for representation, dialogue and transformation, giving a voice to those living on the margins and strengthening their power to act within a fairer, more inclusive society.
<strong>La Converse n’est pas un média r: La Converse is not an inward-looking media outlet. Our mission is rooted in stories created by and for communities that are often ignored, but our content speaks to a much wider audience. The issues we tackle transcend identity boundaries and touch on universal questions. These stories, though grounded in specific experiences, enrich our collective understanding and resonate with a diverse audience.
<strong>La Converse n’est pas un lieu d’: La Converse is not a place of isolation. We are not a media outlet that avoids or shuts out difficult, nuanced conversations. Quite the opposite: we welcome and encourage them, because they are essential to building bridges between people with different perspectives.
<strong>La Converse n’est pas une chambr: La Converse is not an echo chamber. We do not seek to reinforce a single perspective, but to create inclusive spaces where diverse experiences and points of view can engage with one another. We approach issues in all their complexity, without reducing realities to simplistic or binary narratives.
<strong>La Converse n’est pas un média m: La Converse is not an activist media outlet. Journalists from diverse backgrounds are often accused of activism when they cover their own communities, a double standard well documented by many Canadian researchers. At La Converse, we know this accusation is unfounded. Guided by the codes of ethics of the Canadian Association of Journalists and the Fédération professionnelle des journalistes du Québec, we are committed to upholding strict standards of accuracy, fairness and transparency. Our approach is neither partisan nor activist. We practise dialogue journalism, shedding light on issues and connecting diverse perspectives to foster a better understanding of reality.
<strong>Ce qu’est La Converse et pourquo: What La Converse is and why it is essential
La Converse, c’est un média qui a été fo: La Converse is a media outlet founded because many racialized, Indigenous and marginalized communities sorely lack spaces where they can be heard in all their complexity and humanity. We are creating a media space where dialogue is not only possible but central, where nuance is upheld as a core value, and where rich and diverse stories can emerge.
C’est ainsi que nous pouvons réellement: This is how we can truly speak of La Converse as a watchdog of democracy and part of the “fourth estate.” We help strengthen the media ecosystem as a whole.
En tant que média indépendant dirigé par: As an independent media outlet led by racialized women and grounded in rigorous journalistic ethics, La Converse plays a unique role in the media landscape. We amplify where others silence, and we include where others exclude. That is why we take an approach based on dialogue journalism and “bottom-up storytelling,” in which stories emerge from the communities themselves rather than being imposed from above. In addition, our initiatives, such as the Écoles Converse, train the next generation of journalists in an inclusive, decolonized approach, essential to building a fairer and more equitable media future.
Le journalisme ne doit pas seulement inf: Journalism must not only inform, but also question power structures and reflect the full diversity of our society. Without that, our democracy is incomplete. By amplifying forgotten voices, La Converse plays a vital role in the media ecosystem and in society as a whole.
La Converse n’est pas un « ghetto », mai: La Converse is not a “ghetto,” but a bridge. And as our work continues, I hope that more and more people – even those who question our approach – will feel the full power and value of what we are building.
